title: THE BELL THAT TUNED THE CITY
deck: A cathedral has begun to ring itself, forty thousand pilgrims are nine days away, and the tram line beneath it cannot be switched off. Illuminara reads what the tower is already doing, and the ringers and dispatchers have to carry it.
shape: Nine-day countdown in five scenes: a muttering tower and a measured fault, the coupling discovered, a rehearsal that fails by the engineer's own test, a corrected rehearsal with a crowd and a festival morning that maps the crowd's weight, and a festival afternoon that nearly goes wrong.

scenes.title: The Minster Mutters
paragraphs: *Minster and Quay · the ninth evening before the Festival*

At ten past six on the ninth evening before the Festival of Saint Aldric, with the light going copper along the river Orne, the bells in the crossing tower began to talk to themselves. Nobody was in the ringing chamber. Bram Dacey, who had been tower captain for thirty-one years, stood on the belfry stair with one hand on the cold rail and counted. The sound was small: a clapper kissing a sound bow here, another there, the fourth bell and the fifth and the fourth again, about three taps in every four seconds. It was not music. It was what a bell does when something beneath it will not keep still.

In the works office under the roof, Dr. Ravi Taneja had the same rhythm on two screens, drawn as a line. He was the Minster's structural engineer, and he had not slept well since the Riverside extension opened eleven days ago and Line 7 began stopping at the Quay, a hundred and forty metres from the west door. He laid a pencil on the trace.

**Taneja**  
My limit at the lantern is eight milli-g. Before the line opened this tower never read above a half. At this evening's peak it read six point one. Every spike is a tram braking at the Quay.
He did not look up.

**Taneja**  
At festival crowding I would have said hours of margin. At the rate the peaks are growing I would not promise the hours.

Canon Marit Solvang, master of the fabric, had her answer ready. Forty thousand pilgrims would arrive on the ninth day, the Festival had been kept through plague and a siege, and the Chapter would not cancel it. Hanneke Orr, chief dispatcher of Vessin Trams, leaned on the wall with her arms folded and had hers ready too. On festival day the bridges closed for the procession, and the Quay was the only way into the old town for anyone who could not walk four kilometres. She needed a tram every ninety seconds.

**Hanneke**  
And on an ordinary morning I carry thirty thousand people to work on that line. Tell me which of them to strand.

Illuminara had come because the Canon wrote to her, and Wren Odira had come to keep the clock, because someone had to. She had been a court interpreter before she was anything else, and she began as an interpreter does, by asking what each party would have to believe for the other's sentence to be true. Then she asked Taneja something he had not expected.

**Illuminara**  
When a peak comes, how long does the tower take to build, and how long to forget?

**Taneja**  
Twenty seconds to build. Forty to forget.

**Illuminara**  
So one tram is not the danger. One tram is a push of four seconds, and the tower forgives four seconds. The danger is pushes that arrive in step.

She asked to stand on the lantern gallery for the next tram. The force paths of a masonry tower were legible to her the way a pulse is legible to a doctor: a slow lean of load from the crossing piers to the lantern and back again. She could read what leaned. What it meant was her own interpretation, and she did not ask anyone to take it on trust.

**Illuminara**  
It leans and returns once every one point three five seconds.
she said into Wren's radio.

**Illuminara**  
The lean runs along the line to the Quay, not along the nave. Dr. Taneja, check your axes before the next tram, and write your own number first.

He wrote a number on the margin of the trace and covered it with his hand. At 6:41 a tram braked at the Quay. The line on his screen climbed from three point four to four point two, the period read one point three five, and the dominant axis pointed at the river platform. He took his hand away. The paper said 1.35, in his writing, before the tram had finished stopping. He said nothing, which from Taneja was a form of respect.

scenes.title: Metronomes on a Plank
paragraphs: *Minster works office · at nine*

Hanneke brought the braking logs to the works office at nine, because by then she wanted a verdict more than she wanted to be right. The new Orsolo trams blended electric braking into friction brakes below nine kilometres an hour, and in that handover the controller hunted: release, apply, release, a stutter of about three-quarters of a cycle a second that passengers felt as a shiver and the manufacturer certified as within tolerance. No two trams stuttered alike. Speed and load tuned each one a little differently.

Illuminara asked for the pulse hour, when the timetable brought three trams into the Quay at once. Hanneke pulled it up. The three traces began at point seven one, point seven four and point seven seven cycles a second. In twelve seconds all three were at point seven four.

**Hanneke**  
Their controllers do not talk to each other.

**Illuminara**  
No. The ground does.
Illuminara laid her finger on the clay under the Quay, drawn as a brown band on the engineer's section.

**Illuminara**  
The tower's lean comes down through the piers into this, and out along the rails, and every tram feels it at the wheel. Every stutter tips a little toward it. They are metronomes on a plank, and the tower is the plank. We have been asking what the trams are doing to the tower. The tower is also pulling the trams into step.
Wren, who had written the three frequencies in her book, said.

**Wren**  
So slowing them down?

**Hanneke**  
Slowing shifts each stutter, and the pull of the tower is stronger than the shift.

Hanneke said. She had already tried it. Sanding the rails cut slip but not the hunt. The fault was in firmware, and a firmware change to a braking controller needed eleven weeks of recertification. She could stagger arrivals on an ordinary day. On festival day the crowd made the dwell times, and dwell times made bunches.
Illuminara turned to the other window of the problem.

**Illuminara**  
Captain Dacey. Which bells were talking this evening?

**Bram**  
Four and five.
Bram answered without checking.

**Bram**  
Fourth swings short, one point three three seconds on a small arc. Fifth, one point three eight. Every ringer knows what a bell does on a small arc. It is just a swing.

**Illuminara**  
The tower's period is one point three five. Two of your bells keep the same time within three percent. The Minster is trying to grow itself a damper. Those two are the only parts of it free to move against the lean, and no one is keeping them going.
Taneja was already shaking his head, and Illuminara was glad of it.

**Taneja**  
A tuned mass wants a few percent of the modal mass. I put the lantern mode at three hundred and twenty tonnes. Your whole ring is eleven. If every bell did its job that is three and a half percent, and only two are in tune. Next, the crowd. Eight thousand people in the nave lengthen the period, and a damper tuned to an empty church is a damper tuned to the wrong building. Third, a band of ringers pulling ropes near that frequency is a pump. You propose to bolt a pump to a tower that is drowning.

**Illuminara**  
All of that is true, so I would not use the idea on my say-so. Write the number that kills it.

He wrote two. A rehearsal at four in the morning with the line closed; Hanneke to bunch six trams into the Quay; Bram's band to work the ring. If the lantern peak did not stay under three, or if the tower did not ring down from a bunch in under twenty-five seconds instead of forty, the Festival moved to the Meadow outside the walls and he closed the tower, in writing, over the Canon's signature.

**Taneja**  
A lower peak alone proves nothing. Any trick can shave a peak for one cycle. I want the tower to forget faster.
Canon Marit read it twice and signed.

**Canon Marit**  
And you? What do you do?

**Illuminara**  
I read the tower to a precision nobody else here can, and I tell the ringers which bells it wants. I can also hold the load on the top stage for a short while, a quarter of an hour, perhaps a little more. A festival is twelve hours. It is the ringers' day, and the dispatchers'.

scenes.title: A Damper That Cannot Lose
paragraphs: *Minster ringing chamber · the seventh morning before the Festival, 04:00*

On the seventh morning, at four, twelve ringers stood in the dark with their ropes, and Bram told them what Illuminara had asked: lash the clappers, set the fourth, fifth and sixth swinging on small silent arcs, and keep them going. She had reasoned that every clapper strike was motion wasted as sound, and that silent bells would give the tower everything they had. Hanneke put six trams into the Quay in a bunch.

The trace did not look like the plot of a rescue. Taneja had it on the big screen, a line that should have been a single hump, and it grew two. The peak read five point eight. With the ring still it had read six point two. Then the bunch ended and the line did not fall. It rang down over thirty-eight seconds, two seconds better than nothing.

**Taneja**  
Split peak, no loss.
Taneja said, quietly, because he had written the numbers and did not need to say them.

**Taneja**  
A neat textbook absorber with nowhere for the energy to go.

Illuminara had watched it with her attention along the piers and had seen it before the trace finished drawing itself. The tower pushed, the bells swung up, and then the bells handed the push back, a half-beat late, to a tower that had no way to refuse it. She said so at once.

**Illuminara**  
I was wrong to quiet them. A silent bell can only trade energy with the tower. The mutter we heard that evening was the sound of it leaving: each clapper strike takes a little away and does not give it back. A damper that cannot lose anything is only a second building.

**Taneja**  
You tied your own hands.
Taneja said, and then, grudgingly.

**Taneja**  
You said it before the screen did.
It was Teo Vance, nineteen, the youngest in the band, who found the next thing. He was holding the fifth's rope and said, to nobody in particular.

**Teo**  
I can feel it. When the tram comes, the sally lifts on its own. It's the tower. I could tell you the lean without the screen.
The older ringers looked at him, and Bram, who had felt that lift for thirty-one years without ever giving it a number, said.

**Bram**  
He's right. Every one of us can.

Illuminara knelt on the boards and drew it in chalk, because three people in the room needed to see it and one of them had to be able to say it back. A line for the tower. A line under it for the bell.

**Illuminara**  
Energy comes in through the frame, here, as the lift in the sally. It goes into the bell, which is a weight on a rope. It leaves at the end of the swing, where the clapper hits the bronze, as sound and a little heat. Three places. In, across, out. Last night we closed the out.

**Teo**  
So if the tower lifts the sally and I pull, I'm helping it.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. Then you are the pump Dr. Taneja warned about.

**Teo**  
So I don't pull on the lift.
He worked it out with his hands on the rope while the others watched.

**Teo**  
I let it come up. I give it a half-beat. Then I take the rope on the way back down, and the bell is late on purpose. And the clapper has all that swing to hit with.

**Illuminara**  
Yield on the lift. Pull on the return. Then the bell trails the lantern and fights it. If it works you will see two things on Dr. Taneja's screen, the bell line running behind the lantern line, and the tower forgetting in under twenty-five seconds.
She turned to Taneja.

**Illuminara**  
The ring-down is your number. Not mine.

But the band had been awake twenty-seven hours, and she would not ask a tired ring to do a second rehearsal on nerve. She moved it to the fourth night. Taneja read the numbers, agreed, and kept his veto over the Festival where it was.

scenes.title: Twenty-Nine Hundred Coats
paragraphs: *Minster · the fourth night before the Festival, 03:30*

The Canon had asked the city for a favour, and the city came. On the fourth night, at half past three, twenty-nine hundred people filed into the nave in their coats, the choirs of nine parishes and as many neighbours as they had brought, and sat in the dark under the lantern. Illuminara had asked for them. Their mass was the rehearsal's real test, because the tower with a crowd in it was not the tower that had failed on the seventh morning.
She felt it at once. The period had lengthened from one point three five to one point three seven.

**Illuminara, to Bram**  
The fifth is in tune now, and the fourth is too short. Put the sixth on with the fifth. Let the clappers rock and strike as they want.
Taneja's own estimate of the new frequency arrived twenty seconds later and said the same. Teo, with his hands on the rope, said it a breath before either, in the way a ringer says it.

**Teo**  
She's lifting early.
That was the third voice in agreement, and the only one of the three that had not needed a machine.
Bram called it down the ring in the old tower words.

**Bram**  
Yield. Wait. Now take it.

Twelve people who had spent their lives pulling on the beat learned, in the dark, to give way to a building and then lean in against it. Six trams came into the Quay in a bunch, and the sound that went through the nave was small, a clapper kissing a bow, the fifth and the sixth and the fifth again, a sound like a congregation clearing its throat. The twenty-nine hundred people sat very still. The lantern line rose to two point four and bent over.
Taneja did not look at the peak. He had the two traces laid one over the other and his pencil on the gap between them.

**Taneja**  
The bell runs behind the lantern by a quarter of a swing. Clear as a ruled line.
The pencil moved to the tail.

**Taneja**  
And twenty-one seconds to forget. Under three, under twenty-five, with a crowd in the nave and the worst bunch Hanneke can build.
He sat down and took his hand off the rail.

**Taneja**  
That is damping. I would sign that.

**Illuminara**  
Eight thousand will lengthen the period more. The ring does not cover every case. Bells seven and eight are in reserve for it. And a crowd does not fill a nave in one step.
She looked at Taneja.

**Illuminara**  
So we ask the nave to fill slowly, on the morning, while the trams are quiet, and we measure every step. The band must know the handover from each pair to the next before anyone is in danger.

**Taneja**  
The morning of the Festival. With the congregation in.

**Illuminara**  
With the congregation arriving.

The remaining problem was not a bell. Ilya Brandt, the union's organiser, read the dispatchers' plan to space the Quay arrivals and refused it flatly. The plan would hold laden trams at the previous stop, doors closed, pilgrims standing in them for four minutes, because a tower needed it.

**Ilya**  
My drivers will not hold a full tram for a building.

Hanneke did not argue. She went away with the schedule and came back after an hour with a different one: hold only the empty return trams, at Orsolo Bridge, two minutes at a time, so that no bunch of three could form on the Quay side; laden trams never held.

Ilya read it and then read the second page, which Hanneke had headed Pre-Mortem and which she had written the way she wrote incident reports, in the voice of a woman who already knew how it would go wrong. "One failure I cannot schedule away. If anything stops a laden tram inside the hundred and forty metres before the platform, the trams behind must stop behind it, nose to tail, at the safe gap. Five trams fill the zone. When the front one moves, all five go for the platform together, in a convoy forty seconds long, and every one of them brakes into the Quay. A timetable ninety seconds apart does not survive a stop. That is the morning I would be afraid of." She did not say that it was a fear of hers. It was in the margin in her own hand. "I can hold empties. I cannot hold the people already in the stack."
Ilya signed.

**Ilya**  
That I can sign. An empty tram can stand. And the stack, God help us, we manage by hand.
The Canon had one condition of her own.

**Canon Marit**  
A festival with a tower that mutters. I shall have visitors asking why the cathedral is whispering.

**Teo**  
Tell them it is listening.
Teo said. And then, because he was nineteen and in the Canon's presence.

**Teo**  
Sorry.

**Canon Marit**  
No. That will do.

scenes.title: The Hour After the Mass
paragraphs: *Minster and Quay · Festival day and the following evening*

On the morning of the Festival, from half past seven, the nave filled in steps. Hanneke held the trams to the plan. At each thousand people through the west door Taneja called the period and Illuminara called the pair: fifth and sixth until the nave held five thousand, sixth and seventh at seven thousand, then the longest period of all, one point four one, at nine thousand, when the whole congregation would be standing for the Creed. Bram's bands rotated through the ropes with the handover words, from each pair to the next, yield and wait and take. By the time the procession entered, every number the church was likely to make had a pair of bells and a captain's signature beside it. Taneja's last line on the sheet read: Ring-down twenty-three seconds at nine thousand. Taneja had not smiled, but he had crossed out the word Hours.

The Festival of Saint Aldric opened under a hard blue sky, and for six hours it went the way he had written it down. The procession crossed the old town; the bridges were closed; trams ran every ninety seconds and the empty ones waited at Orsolo Bridge. The bells in the crossing tower muttered through the sermon and the blessings. The lantern read two, three, a high of three point four.
Then the closing Mass ended, and eight thousand seven hundred people, who had all stood for it, began to leave the nave together.

Illuminara had been on the lantern gallery since the Mass began, because a falling crowd was the one thing the rehearsals had not made at this speed. It was not that the building would be in a new state; the bands had qualified every pair down the whole ladder. It was the speed at which the mass was leaving. As the nave emptied the period would shorten, faster than any ramp-down they had walked, and the ringers on the sixth and seventh would be late to hand back to the fifth and sixth. She felt it before Taneja's screen did.

**Illuminara**  
One point four oh. Bram, bring the fifth in now. Yield on this lift, and do not wait for the exit to finish.

At the same moment, at 15:04, a laden tram stopped for a child who had run out of the crowd onto the track, sixty metres short of the platform, inside the zone. The child was unhurt. The paramedics took six minutes to say so, and the driver would not move until they did. Behind her, Hanneke's ninety-second trams came on and stacked up as her pre-mortem had said they would, nose to tail, five of them on one track, full of people who had been standing since dawn, each braking in turn inside the hundred and forty metres.

**Hanneke**  
They are full.
Hanneke said into the radio.

**Hanneke**  
They cannot be held back, and I cannot reorder them. The order belongs to the track. What I own is the gap.

She had two choices, and each had a price. She could keep the followers standing once the front driver was cleared, and let the stack grow while a sixth laden tram came up behind it, a longer wait and a longer convoy later. Or she could release the five at the shortest separation the signals would safely allow, forty seconds from first to last, and take the braking burst at the Quay now, while the lantern was still the stronger for the fifth bell being in. She chose the second, because the first only made the burst larger.

At 15:10 the front driver was cleared and the front tram moved. The convoy followed at the minimum safe interval and braked into the Quay in a tight line, and the stutter of five controllers fell into step on the clay. Taneja was calling the number into the radio, not looking at it.

**Taneja**  
Six point eight, at 15:12. Seven point one. Seven point four.
at 15:13, and then the number he had written on the first night: if the lantern held above seven and a half for thirty seconds, he would call the evacuation of the nave and the square.

The ringers were halfway through the handover. The fifth and sixth were in tune with a period that was already gone, and the seventh was still ringing against a nave that was nearly empty. Illuminara put her hands on the cold stone, found the line where the lean was loading the lantern, and took it. She turned the load aside through the piers to the crossing arches, which could carry more than they had ever been asked to. The lantern line on the screen, which had been climbing, hung where it was.

**Wren**  
Fifteen minutes is the most she has.
Wren said into the radio, as she had said numbers into other radios, in a level voice.

**Wren**  
Two gone.

It was not strength she needed so much as precision, and she had spent nine days learning which stones would hold. It was not a thing she could do for an afternoon. The ringers had to take the tower from her in the time she bought them. In the ringing chamber Bram's third band, with Teo on the fifth, finished the handover, yielded on the lift, took the rope on the return, and kept it. Bell lines ran behind the lantern line on Taneja's screen like the ruled gap on the rehearsal night. The clappers struck. The cluster muttered louder than it had all day, five bells and six and five again, and on the gallery the stone began to give back the lean in smaller and smaller pieces.

At fifteen twenty-six, thirteen minutes in, she let go. Taneja held his breath for the forty seconds the tower should have taken to forget. It forgot in twenty-two. The line read three point one and stayed there, and the tower stood without her.

**Hanneke**  
The Quay is clear.
Hanneke said into the radio.

**Hanneke**  
Next bunch is two. Ilya's holding the empties at the bridge.

Nobody was evacuated. By dusk the trams had carried nineteen thousand pilgrims out of the old town without suspending service, and the lantern had not once crossed seven and a half. The Chapter kept the bells muttering for the evening service, and the pilgrims going down the Quay steps looked back up at the tower and heard it, a sound like a very large building clearing its throat before it sang.

There were costs. The ringers would train a year to keep a watch whenever trams braked in autumn, and Bram's band lost a month of its quiet practice. Hanneke's staggered timetable cost eleven percent of her festival capacity and would run until the new controller software arrived in spring. Taneja's report recommended a proper damper in the lantern, which the Chapter could not afford, and which would be cut from the budget twice before it was built.

At ten past six on the evening after the Festival, with the light going copper along the Orne, the bells began to talk to themselves again. This time, standing on the belfry stair with his hand on the cold rail, Bram Dacey knew what had asked them, and how to answer.
